title: J'accuse!
byline: Abel Gance's 1919 French anti-war silent film; US print PD on all theories as of 2026; modern scores on every accessible copy are the live rights trap.

evidence.note: Published 1919. Under the 1909 Copyright Act, even a US-registered and renewed copyright (28 + 28 = 56 years maximum) would have expired by 1975. CTEA 1998 did not revive already-expired copyrights. No US copyright for this title can remain in force after January 1, 2015 (the URAA-restored 95-year ceiling). As of 2026 this is unambiguous.

J'accuse! (1919) was a silent film; the original release had no synchronized musical score. Every extant playable copy, including the Internet Archive item j-accuse.-1919 (metadata tag: 'Sound'), carries a modern musical accompaniment composed and recorded after 1975. That score is an independent copyrighted work owned by its arranger or the production company that commissioned it, not covered by the print's PD status. Reusers must strip or replace the audio, or independently license the specific accompaniment.

editorial:
J'accuse! (1919) is Abel Gance's feature-length anti-war film made while the First World War was still being fought. Produced by PathÃ© and released in France in April 1919, it follows two soldiers â€” one a married farmer, the other a poet involved with the farmer's wife â€” whose personal rivalry is swallowed by the machinery of industrial warfare. Gance filmed sequences using actual soldiers on brief leave from the front; several men who appeared in the climactic 'return of the dead' sequence, in which mutilated veterans rise and march back to ask the living whether their sacrifices were worthwhile, were killed in action within weeks of filming. The original version ran over three hours and was one of the most technically ambitious French productions of the silent era. Gance returned to the story in 1938 with a synchronized-sound remake â€” a legally distinct work not covered here.

For creators, the 1919 silent print is free in the United States: PathÃ© almost certainly never registered US copyright under the 1909 Act, and even the URAA-restored 95-year term (capped at January 1, 2015) has long since run. The one live rights trap is the musical score. Every accessible copy of this film â€” including the Internet Archive version tagged 'Sound' â€” has had a modern accompaniment composed and recorded after 1975, and that score is its own separate copyright, held by whoever arranged and recorded it. To use the footage cleanly, either commission or license a new score, source a copy whose accompaniment has been cleared, or present the images without audio.
faq: Is the 1919 J'accuse print completely free to use?

The silent print is public domain in the United States â€” the last possible US copyright term (a 95-year URAA-restored term from 1919) expired January 1, 2015. However, virtually every playable copy, including the accessible Internet Archive version, carries a modern musical score that is separately copyrighted. You need to strip or replace the audio, or confirm the specific copy's accompaniment is licensed, before using the footage with sound.
Does the URAA restoration affect this film?

It could have, but no longer does. The URAA (1996) might have restored US copyright for this French film because France still protected it as of January 1, 1996 â€” Abel Gance died in 1981 and French copyright runs approximately to 2051. But any URAA-restored US term is capped at 95 years from publication; that ceiling reached January 1, 2015. As of 2026 the print is public domain on all theories.
